claim_under_test: 'Instant learning is solved, so give the model the smartest action once and it is solved forever, in any environment.' This round asked what the INDEX -- the thing that decides which lesson applies where, named as the single bottleneck by THE_BOTTLENECK_IS_THE_INDEX_NOT_THE_LEARNING_20261116_V1 -- is actually WORTH, once the search that produces its evidence is not starved.
the_reordering_in_one_sentence: The index decides WHICH SEARCH STRATEGY to use; at an adequate budget every strategy solves almost everything, so the index's whole value is 17.4% of act_calls and its value is zero for the 8 instances that cannot be solved at all -- while a perfect transition model would remove 99.58% of them, which is the object the tree names as its goal and explicitly does not contain ('this file does not contain a model' -- canonical/runtime/model_v1.py).
the_wrong_answer_this_replaces: That the index is the single bottleneck because no granularity of its features is injective on the policy's distinction. The non-injectivity is REAL and reproduces exactly (see measured_effect.budget_sweep). What does not follow is that repairing it is the top of the order: the policy distinction it fails to resolve changes cost, not solvability.

measured_effect.instrument: canonical/tools/cross_kind_learning_to_learn_benchmark_v1.py via its own _solve_with, 20 kinds x 3 instances = 60 instances, node_budget swept

budget_sweep.note: solved counts are 'at least one of the five policies solves it'

the_8_that_never_solve.evidence: exhaustive reachable-state enumeration, no node budget, depth cap 14 = the search's own max_depth
the_8_that_never_solve.honest_limit: stack_pushout's reachable space is unbounded (a probe run reached discovery depth 6251 and was stopped at a 50000-state cap), so for those two the claim is 'no goal state reachable within the depth the searcher is allowed', NOT 'unsatisfiable'. The other six are exhausted exactly.
the_8_that_never_solve.what_this_is_not: an instrument artifact: nothing about the policy set, the index, or learning enters these six rows

node_budget_1280.note: every satisfiable instance is solved by at least 4 of the 5 policies; NO instance is solved by exactly one

at_adequate_budget_the_choice_stops_disc.interpretation: The '4/30 solved by exactly one policy' shape that motivated a policy index is a property of STARVED SEARCH, not of the problems. It disappears entirely at 1280 nodes.

instance_sensitivity_survives_but_only_a.result: 13/18 kinds with >=2 solvable instances have a different CHEAPEST policy on a different instance
instance_sensitivity_survives_but_only_a.example: binary_odometer: instance 0 needs 15860 act_calls under its cheapest policy, instance 1 needs 38
instance_sensitivity_survives_but_only_a.interpretation: The tree's instance-sensitivity finding is CONFIRMED and is not a budget artifact. But it names the cheapest policy, not the only working one -- so it is a fact about cost, and it is the one real reason an index could pay.

the_price_of_the_index.currency: act_calls at node_budget=1280 over 52 satisfiable instances
the_price_of_the_index.feasibility_change_from_a_perfect_index: 0.00 percentage points (all 52 already solvable under any of >=4 policies)

the_same_budget_spent_where_it_dominates.why_this_is_the_same_budget: both numbers are act_calls spent by the same runs at the same node budget on the same 52 instances; the only difference is what the calls are FOR -- choosing a strategy versus discovering the transitions the plan is made of

the_discriminating_rows_only.note: a row where all five policies win cannot distinguish any chooser from a coin
the_discriminating_rows_only.verdict: The computed arm beats the control by 2 rows out of 8 and costs 72-120 act_calls to compute. This is NOT evidence that a smarter feature is the frontier; it is the control that killed the claim before it was made. Recorded because the number looked like a win.

injectivity_is_reachable_and_still_worth.question: the tree reports no granularity of its key is injective on the policy distinction; is a deeper effect probe injective?
injectivity_is_reachable_and_still_worth.answer: yes at depth 3, and it does not help
injectivity_is_reachable_and_still_worth.conclusion: Injectivity is purchasable and buys nothing: the injective key answers 1 of 30 held-out rows. Finer is strictly WORSE than coarser on held-out accuracy (8/30 vs 4/30), which reproduces the tree's own reason for a coarse key. A key can be made injective, or transferable, and the measurement says not both -- but the reason it does not matter here is that with adequate search there is nothing left to choose between.

what_was_built.why_nothing_was_built: The measurement that decides the next build is a disagreement between two of the tree's own documents, and it resolves against the more recent one. Building an index repair first would have optimised 17.4% while the dominant term sat named and unbuilt. The law 'the best part is no part' applies to the index repair, this round, on measurement.

corrections_to_my_own_earlier_work_this_: I first measured that a depth-3 effect probe predicts the winning policy 8/8 on discriminating held-out rows, and was about to report it. The attribution control showed always-pick-bfs_lex scores 6/8, so the arm's real gain is 2 rows. The claim was killed before publication; both numbers are kept above.

I first wrote that 8 of 60 instances are UNSATISFIABLE. Exhaustive enumeration proves that for 6 of them (state space exhausted, <=27 states) and does NOT prove it for the 2 stack_pushout instances, whose reachable space is unbounded and whose goal is merely absent within the allowed depth. The receipt states both.
The claim that the policy index is the single bottleneck does not survive an adequate search budget. The non-injectivity it rests on reproduces exactly; the priority does not follow from it.
honest_limits: Authority NONE. Sandbox measurement on the tree's own synthetic benchmark; not independent verification.
The 20 kinds are the tree's own hand-written generators. 'No policy is the only solver' is a statement about these 20 kinds and 5 search strategies, not about computer use in general.
act_calls is this benchmark's action meter. 99.58% is the ratio of two sums over the same 52 instances; it is not a claim that a transition model is 240x faster anywhere else.
No transition model was built or measured this round. The 99.58% is an UPPER BOUND obtained by substituting the true plan length, not a result from a learner.
stack_pushout instances 0 and 1 are not proven unsatisfiable (unbounded state space).
The depth-3 injective key was computed on instance 0 only when building train tables; held-out scoring used the same instance index for both train and test rows.
laws: A cheaper way to CHOOSE among strategies that all work is not the same as a way to SOLVE what none of them solves.
An index's value is the regret of the best fixed choice. Measure that before repairing the index.
A feature that separates perfectly on the data it was built on is a fingerprint. Injectivity and transferability must be scored separately, on held-out kinds.
When a benchmark says 'no policy solves this', enumerate the reachable state space before believing a policy could.
The best part is no part: the highest-value action this round was not building the repair that the previous document recommended.
